q-131461.worked_solution:
As $x$ approaches $1$ from the left, the function $g(x)$ approaches $1.$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}g(x)=1.
$$

Likewise, as $x$ approaches $1$ from the right, the function $g(x)$ approaches $0.$ Therefore,

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}g(x)=0.
$$

In conclusion, we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{-}}g(x)=1,\,{lim}_{x\to \,{1}^{+}}g(x)=0.
$$

q-131464.worked_solution:
On the left side of the graph, we see that as the values of $x$ decrease and approach $-\infty ,$ the graph of the function $g(x)$ moves closer and closer to the horizontal asymptote $y=-1.$

Consequently, $g(x)$ approaches the value $-1$ as $x$ approaches $-\infty ,$ and we have

$$
{lim}_{x\to -\infty }g(x)=-1.
$$

On the right side of the graph, as the values of $x$ increase and approach $\infty ,$  the graph of the function $g(x)$ moves closer and closer to the horizontal asymptote $y=-1.$ Therefore, 

$$
{lim}_{x\to \infty }g(x)=-1.
$$

q-131466.worked_solution:
According to the sum and constant multiple rules, we can compute the required limit as follows:

$$
{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}(5f(x)+6g(x)+3{x}^{3})=5{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}f(x)+6{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}g(x)+3{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}{x}^{3}
$$

 

The above equation assumes that ${lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}f(x)$ and ${lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}g(x)$ both exist.

From the graph, we see ${lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}f(x)=0,$ and from part 3, we found ${lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}g(x)=1.$ So, we have  

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}(5f(x)+6g(x)+3{x}^{3}) & =5{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}f(x)+6{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}g(x)+3{lim}_{x\to \,(-1)}{x}^{3} \\  & =5\cdot 0+6\cdot 1+3\cdot (-1)^{3} \\  & =0+6-3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

limx→(−1)(5f(x)+6g(x)+3x3)=5limx→(−1)f(x)+6limx→(−1)g(x)+3limx→(−1)x3

The above equation assumes that limx→(−1)f(x) and limx→(−1)g(x) both exist.

From the graph, we see limx→(−1)f(x)=0, and from part 3, we found limx→(−1)g(x)=1. So, we have

limx→(−1)(5f(x)+6g(x)+3x3)=5limx→(−1)f(x)+6limx→(−1)g(x)+3limx→(−1)x3=5⋅0+6⋅1+3⋅(−1)3=0+6−3=3.
